## Why an academic website?

- Showcase your work, publications, projects, ...
- It's *yours*, you can take it with you (unlike institutional pages)
- A central place where people can find you and your research

## Tools for academic websites

**Many tools exist for static websites, today we use Quarto**

- Simple, works in RStudio / Positron / VS Code
- Easy to publish for free
- Excellent [documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/)

## What a finished site can look like

Some examples of academic Quarto websites:

::: nonincremental

- [Silvia Canelón](https://silviacanelon.com/)
- [Andrew Heiss](https://www.andrewheiss.com/)
- [Sam Csik](https://samanthacsik.github.io/)

:::

## Follow along

To follow along you only need:

- Recent version of RStudio (or Positron, VS Code)
- GitHub account (for publishing, optional)

## What is Quarto?

. . .

> Quarto is an open-source scientific and technical publishing system

. . .

Examples of document types that can be created with Quarto:

::: {.nonincremental}

-   **Documents**: HTML, PDF, Word
-   **Presentations**: HTML, Powerpoint
-   **Books**: HTML, ePub, PDF
-   **Websites**: HTML
- ...

:::

## What is Quarto?

- A Quarto document (`.qmd`) has three components:
  - **Markdown** text
  - (Optional) **code** chunks (R, Python, Julia, ...)
  - **YAML** header for metadata
- You **render** the project → Quarto turns `.qmd` files into HTML, PDF, etc.

. . .

A Quarto *website* is just: **several `.qmd` files + one `_quarto.yml` config file**

## What we won't cover today

::: nonincremental

- Executing code in documents (R/Python output)
- PDF/Word documents or slides
- Advanced theming/CSS
- Custom domains

:::

. . .

All of these are possible with Quarto. Pointers at the end!

# Build a website from scratch {.inverse}

> Understanding the basics before we use the template

## Building from scratch

I'll create a minimal website live. **No need to follow along**, just watch.

. . .

::: nonincremental

The steps:

1. Create a new Quarto Website project in RStudio
2. Look at the generated files
3. Render and preview
4. Add a new page

:::

## The core loop

After the demo, this is the mental model:

. . .

::: nonincremental

- A Quarto website = a **folder of `.qmd` files** + **`_quarto.yml`**
- Add a page = **create a `.qmd`** + **add it to the navbar** in `_quarto.yml`
- See your changes = **click Render**

:::

. . .

That's it. Everything else builds on this.

# Customize the template {.inverse}

> From template to your personal website

## Switching to the template

- We *could* build everything from scratch, but we'd run out of time
- I prepared a **template** with more pages and nicer defaults
- It's just what we built, with more content

. . .

**From now on: follow along with me!**

. . .

::: nonincremental

1. Download the template from the link in chat
2. Unzip and open the `.Rproj` file in RStudio
3. Click **Render** to see the template site

:::

## Template file structure

::: nonincremental

| File / Folder | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `_quarto.yml` | Site-wide config (navbar, theme, footer) |
| `index.qmd` | Home page (set up as an About page) |
| `cv.qmd` | CV page |
| `publications.qmd` | Publications page |
| `blog.qmd` + `posts/` | Blog listing + individual posts |
| `styles.css` | Small custom style tweaks |

:::

## Exercise: `_quarto.yml` {.inverse}

::: nonincremental

> :pencil2: **Exercise (3 min):**
>
> 1. Change the site `title:` to your name
> 2. Pick a theme from the [theme list](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html) and swap the `theme:` value
> 3. Render and see what changed

:::

## Exercise: `index.qmd` (the About page) {.inverse}

Quarto has a special **About page** type, perfect for a personal landing page.

::: nonincremental

- `template:` choose from [several layouts](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-about.html) (jolla, trestles, solana, marquee, broadside)
- `image:` path to your photo
- `links:` social/email links with icons

:::

. . .

::: nonincremental

> :pencil2: **Exercise (4 min):**
>
> 1. Replace the placeholder text with a short bio
> 2. Update the `links:`, delete what doesn't apply, add your own
> 3. (Optional) Try a different `template:` and re-render

:::

## Exercise: `cv.qmd` {.inverse}

A page can be very simple: just a YAML header with a title and markdown content.

::: nonincremental

> :pencil2: **Exercise (3 min):**
>
> 1. Replace the placeholder content with your own CV
> 2. (Or just a few lines, you can finish later)

:::

## `publications.qmd`

- Same idea as the CV: markdown content grouped by year
- Write citations by hand, optionally with links

. . .

:bulb: If you have many publications, you can later switch to a `.bib` file with automatic formatting. See the [Quarto docs on citations](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html).

## Listing pages: `blog.qmd` + `posts/`

A **listing page** shows a collection of other pages. Perfect for blogs, talks, or projects.

. . .

::: nonincremental

- `blog.qmd` has a `listing:` block in the YAML:
  - `contents: posts` → look in the `posts/` folder
  - `type: default` → layout style (`default`, `grid`, `table`)
  - `sort: "date desc"` → newest first
- Each post lives in its own subfolder in `posts/` with an `index.qmd`

:::

## Exercise: Add a blog post {.inverse}

::: nonincremental

> :pencil2: **Exercise (5 min):**
>
> 1. Create a new folder in `posts/`, add an `index.qmd` with a title, date, and a few lines of text
> 2. Render and check that it appears in the blog listing
> 3. (Optional) Try changing `type: default` to `type: grid` in `blog.qmd`

:::

## (Optional) Custom styling with SCSS

Themes are a starting point. If you want to tweak colors, fonts, or spacing, you can use SCSS.

Wire it into `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
format:
  html:
    theme: [cosmo, custom.scss]
```

. . .

::: nonincremental

- **Want to go further?**
  - [Quarto theming docs](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html#theme-options)
  - Pick colors with [coolors.co](https://coolors.co) or [Adobe Color](https://color.adobe.com)

:::

# Publish your website {.inverse}

> Getting your site online

## How publishing works

::: nonincremental

1. When you **render**, Quarto produces a folder of HTML, CSS, and image files
2. A **hosting service** stores those files and serves them at a public URL
3. That's the entire concept: **render → upload → live**

:::

. . .

**Options:** GitHub Pages, Netlify, Posit Connect Cloud, university web server, ...

Today we use **GitHub Pages**: free, reliable, and standard in academia.

## Publishing to GitHub Pages

::: nonincremental

Three steps:

1. Tell Quarto to **render to `docs/`** by adding `output-dir: docs` in `_quarto.yml`
2. **Push to GitHub**: create a repo and push your project
3. **Turn on Pages** in the repo settings

:::

. . .

Your site will be live at `https://<username>.github.io/<reponame>/`

## Step 1: Render to `docs/`

Add this to `_quarto.yml`:

```yaml
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
```

Then render again.

## Step 2: Push to GitHub

- I'll demo this with **GitHub Desktop** (easiest for beginners)
- If you use Git from the terminal or RStudio, that works too

. . .

::: nonincremental

1. Open GitHub Desktop → **Add Existing Repository** (or create new)
2. Commit all files
3. **Publish repository** to GitHub

:::

## Step 3: Turn on GitHub Pages

::: nonincremental

On your GitHub repo page:

1. **Settings** → **Pages** (left sidebar)
2. Source: **Deploy from a branch**
3. Branch: **main**, folder: **/docs**
4. Click **Save**
5. Wait ~1-2 min → your site is live :tada:

:::

## Exercise: Publish your website {.inverse}

::: nonincremental

> :pencil2: **Now you: publish your website!**
>
> Follow the three steps. If your site is live, **drop the URL in the chat**!
>
> If you don't have Git set up, follow along conceptually. I'll share a written guide with screenshots so you can finish at your own pace.

:::

## Updating your site later

The workflow from now on:

::: nonincremental

1. **Edit** your `.qmd` files
2. **Render**
3. **Commit and push** (Git pane or GitHub Desktop)
4. GitHub rebuilds automatically, changes are live in ~1 min

:::

. . .

That's it. Welcome to having a website. :tada:
